I've been working this land for 38 years. I know Quzhou's conditions — the alkaline sandy soil, the dry springs, the hot summers. My well gives me control that rain-fed farmers don't have, and I rely on that. At 64, it's just me and my wife, so I have to be realistic about labor. Cotton is the hardest work, but the price has been reasonable and I know how to handle it.

My 10.1 mu is split the way I've always done it — 6 mu in the wheat-maize double crop, 4.1 mu in cotton. The wheat-maize land cycles every year, the cotton stays on its own plot. I see no reason to change this arrangement. I've tried expanding cotton before and it wore us out at harvest.

For **wheat**, I plant in mid-October after ploughing under the maize stubble. I use the same improved variety I've planted for years — Jimai series. Reliable, decent yield, familiar disease resistance profile for our local stripe rust. I split my nitrogen: base dressing before sowing, topdress at jointing. I irrigate at sowing if the soil is dry, then wintering, jointing, and heading — four times is my normal. Three pesticide sprays: pre-emergent herbicide, aphid and rust control in spring.

For **maize**, I go in immediately after wheat harvest in early June — no time to waste. Hybrid seed, always. Rotary till the stubble rather than plough — saves time, and my back isn't what it was. I put nitrogen down in two shots: base plus big bell. Three irrigations: at planting if dry, jointing, and silking. Two pesticide applications — herbicide early, and one spray for corn borer if pressure is there.

For **cotton**, I plough in spring and transplant in late April. Hybrid seed. Cotton drinks potassium, so I push that up compared to the grain crops. Five pesticide applications — bollworm, aphids, whitefly pressure here is real. Four irrigations, timed to squaring, boll set, and boll opening. This is where most of our labor goes.
